newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole trade broadsides on ethics.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole trade broadsides on ethics.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and challenger Bob Dole exchanged broadsides on Saturday with Clinton still retaining a comfortable lead and with momentum moving toward a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives.

Dole referred to questionable contributions to the Democratic Party from people associated with interests in Indonesia and South Korea and said: "Because integrity is everything, we cannot allow political influence of any American to be outweighed by foreign money."
The Democratic National Committee on Friday relieved the fund raising duties of its finance vice chairman John Huang.
Dole made his accusations in his weekly radio address and at a rally in Somerset, Kentucky. He leveled similar ethics charges earlier in the week.
The Clinton campaign was quick to respond and said: "Bob Dole should take time to concentrate on the ethical problems in his own campaign."

The statement by a Clinton-Gore campaign spokesman said Dole had been silent on his finance vice chairman Simon Firemen who pleaded guilty to illegally reimbursing his employees for contribution to the Dole campaign.

Spokesman Joe Lockhart said Dole had not talked about money laundered through Hong Kong banks to promote his own campaign and on cases in Pennsylvania and Nevada where funds were probably illegally funnelled to his campaign.
Clinton, in his weekly radio address on Saturday, emphasised ways to cut drug and alcohol use by teens, both likely to get the backing of people with children.
He proposed requiring teens to pass a drug test to get a driver's license and to take away their license if they drink and drive or as a sanction for other drug offences.
The president, in Washington on Saturday, was expected to return to the campaign trail next week, opening a four-day bid for votes in New York, New Jersey, Ohio, Michigan and Florida.
He goes on the trail with a lead over Dole of 44.6 percent to 36.8, according to Reuters daily tracking poll on Saturday, down from 43.6 percent to 34.6 percent on Friday.
Poll taker John Zogby Group International said Dole's gain in the survey, which uses a three-day rolling average, reflected a bounce up after Wednesday's presidential debate.
Zogby predicted the poll on Sunday would show a further gain for Dole. Dole also gained ground after the first debate with Clinton but that increase soon disappeared.
With elections less than three weeks to go momentum has swung to Demcrats in Congressional elections, putting them in range of regaining control of the House of Representatives.
Political experts said a House victory was within reach of the Democrats, but Republicans seemed likely to retain their control of the Senate.
Republicans hold a 235-198 majority in the House and a 53-47 lead in the Senate.

The thinking had been that Republicans would retain control of both sides, but with the wide lead Clinton now enjoys as a head of his ticket, the president's vote-pulling ability could also mean a House victory for the Democats.
But a Senate victory seems less likely, the experts say.
Zogby said a 10 percent lead for Clinton could translate into a House victory, but it would take a 13 percent margin for a victory in the Senate.
